prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures a steep top-down egocentric view where the camera wearer stands above a mulch and broken-concrete ground plane (~1.5–2.0 m below the camera), flanked by a green trash bin to the bottom-left (~1.0–1.5 m away) and a low concrete ledge to the right (~0.8–1.4 m away). The brightest, nearest surfaces are the wearer's own torso and arms (~0.15–0.5 m), which shift across the five frames as the left hand moves from ~0.6 m ahead-left in frame 1, up to ~0.15–0.25 m directly in front of the camera in frame 2, and then forward in frames 3–5 (~0.4–0.6 m) to join the right hand holding a suspended blue demolition hammer within arm's reach (~0.4–0.7 m in front-right, ~0.8–1.2 m above the feet). Meanwhile, a child enters from the top-left on the mulch (~1.8–2.0 m away from the camera and ~1.0 m from the wearer's feet in frames 1–2, facing right toward the wearer's legs), moves closer in frames 3–4 (~1.2–1.5 m from the camera, partially occluded behind the wearer's raised left arm), and in frame 5 reaches an arm upward (~0.6–1.0 m away) to touch the tool's front handle right next to the wearer's left hand without looking up at the camera. Compared to RGB alone, the depth map makes it much easier to separate the vertical layering between the held power tool and raised arms in the near foreground (~0.3–0.7 m) and the wearer's legs, feet, and ground directly beneath them (~1.0–1.8 m), as well as the continuous 3D slope of the child's arm reaching up to the handle in frame 5. However, the map is unreliable in the dark upper-left background where the ground and the approaching child (~1.5–2.0 m) are compressed into nearly uniform black during frames 1–4, and it exhibits a sharp vertical seam artifact across the wearer's chest in frame 1 while smoothing over the internal geometry of the tool.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map attempts to isolate people in the top-down scene—where the camera wearer's torso, arms, and legs occupy the central and right foreground (~0.15–1.5 m from the camera) and a second person (a child) moves from the top-left background (~1.8–2.0 m away in frames 1–2) toward the wearer's legs and held demolition hammer (~1.0–1.5 m from the camera in frames 3–5, within arm's reach of both people). Across the sequence, the masks reflect the large foreground rearrangement as the wearer's left arm rises close to the lens in frame 2 (~0.15–0.25 m) and then extends forward in frames 3–5 (~0.4–0.6 m) to grasp the front handle of the tool held on the right, partially occluding the child beneath the left arm in frames 4–5. Beyond roughly silhouetting the foreground body parts against the background, the map adds little that is hard to see in RGB and is largely unreliable because it splits the single camera wearer into two to four separate 'person' instances bounded by artificial vertical seams. It also completely fails to segment the blue demolition hammer held within arm's reach (~0.4–0.7 m)—except for misclassifying its front handle in frame 1 as a 'cell phone'—and omits the green trash bin on the left (~1.0–1.5 m) and the orange cord on the top-right. Furthermore, the child who approaches from the top-left and reaches up to the tool handle is missed in frame 1, only partially captured at the top-left edge in frames 2–3, and merged into the wearer's left-arm mask or lost under occlusion in frames 4–5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is almost entirely blank across the five-frame strip, detecting only the camera wearer's extended left hand in frame 1 (~0.6 m ahead and to the left of the camera) and a single yellow body skeleton in frame 4 (~1.2–1.5 m below and ahead of the camera). In context with the RGB strip, the magenta hand skeleton in frame 1 shows the wearer's left fingers curled near the green trash bin (~1.0–1.5 m on the left) while the right hand holds the demolition hammer (~0.6–0.8 m on the right), and the yellow skeleton in frame 4 localizes the child crouched near the wearer's feet (~0.3–0.5 m in front of the shins) facing rightward toward the tool while partially occluded beneath the wearer's left forearm. The articulated keypoints in frame 1 make the exact finger flexion of the wearer's left hand slightly clearer than in the motion-blurred RGB image, and the frame 4 skeleton confirms the presence and rightward body orientation of the heavily occluded child beneath the wearer's arm. However, the pose map is highly unreliable for this steep egocentric viewpoint: it completely misses the camera wearer's torso, legs, and right arm in every frame, as well as the wearer's left hand when it moves within ~0.15–0.25 m of the head in frame 2 and onto the tool handle at ~0.4–0.6 m in frames 3–5. It also fails to track the second person entering from the top-left (~1.8–2.0 m) in frames 1–3 and misses both people's hands when they simultaneously grasp the tool's front handle within ~0.5 m of the camera in frame 5.
